The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter

When my mother left, my father took the only job he could find that would keep us together: keeper of the lighthouse on Carrick Point. I was eleven and furious. The nearest shop was an hour's walk away, the nearest girl my age lived on the mainland, and the school sent my lessons by post, in a brown envelope that arrived every second Tuesday with the supply boat.

My father was not a talkative man. He believed that most things could be explained with a pencil and the back of an envelope, and he drew diagrams of everything – the tides, the lamp, the reason the wind always seemed to blow straight through my bedroom wall. At first I refused to look at them. Later, when there was nothing else to look at, I began to keep them in a shoebox under my bed.

The light itself was his whole world. Every evening at sunset he climbed the hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room, polished the great glass lens until it shone, and wound the clockwork that turned it. If the clockwork stopped, he had to turn the lens by hand, all night, so that the ships could still recognise our signal: two long flashes and one short. "Every lighthouse speaks its own language," he told me. "If ours goes silent, a captain could think he is somewhere else."

That winter the clockwork broke during the worst storm in forty years. The radio was dead, the boat could not come, and my father had a fever so high that he could hardly stand. So I climbed the stairs myself. I had watched him often enough. For nine hours I pushed the heavy handle round and round, counting the flashes aloud – long, long, short – until my arms shook and my voice disappeared.

At dawn a fishing boat came into the bay, and its captain walked up to the house with a bag of oranges. He had seen our light all night, he said, and it had brought him home. He never knew who had been turning it.

My father recovered. He did not say much, but the next brown envelope from school contained, along with my maths, a diagram in his handwriting: a girl, a handle and a ship, connected by a long, careful line.

(Vadbeno besedilo Piflar.si)

  1. 0.Where did the narrator's family live?
    In a lighthouse (on Carrick Point).
  2. 1.Why did the father accept the job at the lighthouse?
  3. 2.How did the narrator receive her school lessons?
  4. 3.What did the father use to explain things?
  5. 4.Where did the narrator keep her father's drawings?
  6. 5.What did the father do to the lens every evening?
  7. 6.What was the lighthouse's signal?
  8. 7.Why was it important that the light did not go silent?
  9. 8.Why couldn't the father turn the lens himself during the storm?
  10. 9.How long did the narrator turn the handle?
  11. 10.What did the captain bring to the house?
  12. 11.How did the father show his gratitude?

1. To keep the family together. / So they could stay together.
2. By post. / In an envelope (by post).
3. (Pencil-drawn) diagrams. / A pencil and an envelope.
4. In a shoebox (under her bed).
5. He polished it.
6. Two long flashes and one short (flash).
7. A captain could get lost. / Captains could think they were elsewhere.
8. He had a (high) fever. / He was ill.
9. (For) nine hours.
10. A bag of oranges.
11. With a diagram (in the envelope). / He drew her a diagram.
naloge.razlaga:
1. To keep the family together. / So they could stay together.
»the only job he could find that would keep us together« – namen, zato odgovor z to + nedoločnik ali so (that).
2. By post. / In an envelope (by post).
»the school sent my lessons by post« – dovolj je način: by post.
3. (Pencil-drawn) diagrams. / A pencil and an envelope.
»most things could be explained with a pencil and the back of an envelope« in »drew diagrams of everything«.
4. In a shoebox (under her bed).
Neposredno iz besedila: »keep them in a shoebox under my bed«.
5. He polished it.
»polished the great glass lens until it shone« – vprašanje sprašuje le po leči, ne po urnem mehanizmu.
6. Two long flashes and one short (flash).
»two long flashes and one short« – zapiši celoten vzorec.
7. A captain could get lost. / Captains could think they were elsewhere.
»a captain could think he is somewhere else« – odgovor parafraziraš v 1–5 besedah.
8. He had a (high) fever. / He was ill.
»a fever so high that he could hardly stand«.
9. (For) nine hours.
»For nine hours I pushed the heavy handle round«.
10. A bag of oranges.
»walked up to the house with a bag of oranges«.
11. With a diagram (in the envelope). / He drew her a diagram.
Oče ne govori veliko, hvaležnost pokaže z risbo: »a diagram in his handwriting: a girl, a handle and a ship«.

Why we queue: a short history of standing in line

Few habits are as British as waiting your turn – but the queue is younger than you might think.

Visitors to Britain are often amazed by the patience of people at bus stops, [0]. The orderly queue has become part of the national image, yet historians say that for most of history people simply pushed.

The modern queue appeared in the early nineteenth century, when industrial towns grew rapidly and large crowds began to gather at shops, ticket offices and factory gates. Before that time, most people bought what they needed at markets, [1].

The habit really took root during the Second World War. Food was rationed, and every family received a book of coupons [2]. Waiting in line became a patriotic duty, and government posters encouraged people to "take your turn". Anyone who pushed in front risked the anger of the whole street.

Psychologists say that queues work because they feel fair. We are willing to wait for a long time as long as we believe that everybody is treated equally. What makes us furious is not the waiting itself [3]. Experiments show that people in a slow line become more stressed when a second, faster line opens next to them, even if their own wait does not get any longer.

Shops and theme parks have learned to use this knowledge. Some put mirrors near lifts, [4]. Others display a waiting time that is a little longer than the real one, so that customers are pleasantly surprised [5]. Disney even hires designers to plan queues that bend around corners, which prevents visitors from seeing how many people are still in front of them.

Technology is now changing the queue once again. Many restaurants send a text message when a table is ready, [6]. Online, we wait in "virtual queues" to buy concert tickets, watching a little figure walk slowly across the screen.

Some experts believe that the traditional line will soon disappear. Others are not so sure. Standing in a queue, they argue, is a small social ritual [7]. It is one of the few moments when strangers agree on a rule without anyone telling them to.

Whatever happens, the British are unlikely to give up their reputation without a fight. A recent survey found that nine out of ten adults still feel embarrassed [8]. Perhaps the queue will survive simply because nobody wants to be the first [9].

  2. Bbut the feeling that someone else is getting an advantage
  3. Cwhen they see somebody ignoring the line
  4. Dbecause watching your own reflection makes the wait seem shorter
  5. Ewhere bargaining and shouting were part of the fun
  6. Fso that customers can go for a walk instead of standing at the door
  7. Gto break this unwritten rule
  8. Hthat reminds us we are part of a community
  9. Iwhen the doors finally open
  10. Jwho wait calmly in the rain
  11. Kalthough nobody has ever measured it
  12. Lwhen the line moves faster than they expected

2. A
3. B

Pred vrzeljo so »markets«; oziralni »where« uvaja opis tržnic, kjer so barantali – nasprotje urejenega čakanja.
2. A
»a book of coupons [2]« – kuponi so omogočali nakup določene količine živil (which allowed them …).
3. B
»not the waiting itself [3]« zahteva drugi del zveze not … but …: but the feeling …
4. D
Ogledala ob dvigalih: razlog z because – odsev skrajša občutek čakanja.
5. L
»pleasantly surprised [5]« – presenečeni so, ko se vrsta premika hitreje, kot so pričakovali.
6. F
SMS, ko je miza prosta – gostje zato ne čakajo pred vrati (so that …).

»a small social ritual [7]« + oziralni stavek that reminds us … community.
8. C
»feel embarrassed [8]« – zadrega, ko vidijo nekoga, ki ne spoštuje vrste.
9. G
»the first [9]« + to + nedoločnik: the first to break this unwritten rule.

How the bicycle changed women's lives

In the 1890s, Europe and America were gripped by a cycling craze. For the first time, the bicycle was cheap, safe and (0) (COMFORT) enough to be used by ordinary people – and women were among its most (1) (ENTHUSIASM) riders.

Before the bicycle, a woman's freedom of movement was (2) (SEVERE) limited. She usually needed a carriage, a horse or a male companion to travel any distance. Cycling offered a new kind of (3) (DEPEND): with a machine that cost about as much as a month's wages, a young woman could visit friends, go to work or explore the countryside alone.

Not everyone welcomed this change. Doctors warned of a mysterious illness called "bicycle face", supposedly caused by the (4) (EXHAUST) of keeping one's balance. Newspapers printed cartoons that showed female cyclists as (5) (RESPONSIBLE) mothers who neglected their homes. Some critics even claimed that cycling would make women (6) (ABLE) to have children.

The bicycle also caused a (7) (REVOLVE) in fashion. Long skirts and tight corsets made pedalling almost impossible, so many riders adopted loose trousers called "bloomers". To many observers they looked shockingly (8) (APPROPRIATE), and women who wore them were sometimes insulted in the street.

Despite the (9) (OPPOSE), the number of female cyclists continued to grow. Cycling clubs organised long-distance rides, and in 1895 the American (10) (CAMPAIGN) Susan B. Anthony said that the bicycle had done more to free women than anything else in the world. In Britain, a young woman named Annie Londonderry became an international (11) (CELEBRATE) after cycling around the world in fifteen months.

Historians now see the bicycle as an important step towards political (12) (EQUAL). It gave women physical confidence, helped them meet and organise, and made the idea of a woman travelling alone seem (13) (ORDINARILY) rather than scandalous. As one suffragist wrote, a woman on a bicycle was a picture of (14) (FREE) that nobody could forget. More than a century later, the image has lost none of its (15) (SIGNIFY).

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Today we remember a woman whose name was almost forgotten for more than a century: Mary Anning, who was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the Dorset coast. Her family was poor. Her father, Richard, was a carpenter who earned a little extra money by selling curiosities – shells and strange stones – to tourists who came to the seaside in summer.

The cliffs around Lyme Regis are made of soft rock that slips into the sea after every storm, and with each landslide new fossils appear. Richard took Mary and her brother Joseph along the beach to collect them. When he died in 1810, he left the family in debt, and fossil hunting turned from a hobby into the family's main income.

In 1811, Joseph found a strange skull. Over the next months, Mary, who was only twelve, uncovered the rest of the skeleton. It was an ichthyosaur, a marine reptile, and it was the first complete one ever identified. Later she discovered the first plesiosaur skeleton, an animal with a tiny head and an extremely long neck. When the French scientist Georges Cuvier saw the drawings, he thought it must be a fake. A meeting of experts was called, and only after they had examined the bones did Cuvier admit that he had been wrong.

Mary had almost no formal education, but she taught herself geology and anatomy. She even dissected modern fish and cuttlefish to understand the animals she was digging up. Gentlemen scientists visited her shop to ask for her opinion, yet when they published papers about her finds, her name was usually missing. As a woman, she could not join the Geological Society of London, and she was not allowed to attend its meetings.

The work was dangerous. In 1833, a landslide killed her dog, Tray, only a few metres away from her. Mary carried on working until she died of breast cancer in 1847, at the age of forty-seven.

Today, her story is told in museums, in children's books and even in a feature film. In 2010, the Royal Society named her one of the ten British women who have most influenced the history of science, and in 2022 a statue of her was finally unveiled in Lyme Regis.

Mary Anning

You will hear an interview with Tom Blake, who keeps bees on the roofs of London. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Tom, you look after bees in the middle of London. How did that start?

Tom: By accident, really. I was working in an office in the City, and one day a swarm landed on the window of our meeting room. Nobody knew what to do, so I phoned a beekeeper, and I was fascinated by how calmly she collected them. Within a year I had done a course and had two hives on my own balcony.

Interviewer: And now?

Tom: Now I manage about sixty hives on the roofs of hotels, banks and a hospital. Companies pay me to keep the bees, and in return they get honey with their own label. Many of them use it as a present for clients.

Interviewer: Isn't a city a strange place for bees?

Tom: People think so, but London is full of parks, private gardens and railway embankments. There is a greater variety of flowers than in the countryside, where you often have huge fields of just one crop. That's why city honey usually tastes more complex – every jar is a mixture of hundreds of plants.

Interviewer: Is there a downside?

Tom: Yes, and it's an important one. There are now so many hives in central London that there isn't enough food for all the bees, especially in late summer. Honeybees then compete with wild bees, and wild bees lose. So I tell companies that are thinking of getting hives: plant flowers first. A roof garden helps more than another hive.

Interviewer: What does a typical day look like for you?

Tom: In spring I open every hive once a week to check that the queen is laying eggs and that the colony isn't preparing to swarm. A strong colony can have fifty thousand bees, and if they swarm from a hotel roof onto a busy street, you get calls from the police. The hardest part of the job is carrying equipment up the stairs – most of these buildings don't let you use the lifts.

Interviewer: Do you get stung?

Tom: All the time! About once a day in summer. You stop reacting after a while, although I always carry medicine in case a visitor is allergic.

Interviewer: Finally, what is the most important thing your bees have taught you?

Tom: Patience. You can't hurry bees. If you move fast, they get nervous. So I've learned to slow down, which, for someone who used to work in finance, is quite a change.

An interview with a beekeeper

You recently took part in a week-long project at your school in which students organised a repair café, a place where people from the town could bring broken objects to be fixed for free.

Write a report of 120–150 words to the head teacher, in which you:

  • explain which part of the project was the most successful and why,
  • suggest how the project could be improved next year.

naloge.rezultat: Formalno poročilo z glavo in naslovom, uvodom z namenom, tremi odstavki s podnaslovi (kaj so prinesli in popravili, najuspešnejši del z razlogom, predlog za izboljšavo) in kratkim sklepom; 120–150 besed, formalni jezik.
naloge.razlaga:
Zgradba poročila
To: the Head Teacher / From: Dominik(a) Novak / Subject: Repair café project
Poročilo ima glavo (komu, od koga, zadeva) in naslov. Ni nagovora »Dear …« kot pri pismu.
Introduction – The aim of this report is to summarise the repair café organised by our class last week.
Uvod v eni povedi pove namen poročila.
Odstavek 1: kaj so prinesli
Over 60 visitors brought items such as lamps, toasters, bicycles and torn jackets. Our volunteers managed to repair around 40 of them.
Prva iztočnica: konkretne stvari in številke. Vsaka iztočnica dobi svoj odstavek s podnaslovom.
Odstavek 2: najuspešnejši del
The most successful part was the bicycle corner, because it attracted families and many visitors learned to fix punctures themselves.
Druga iztočnica zahteva dva dela: kaj in zakaj (because, as a result).
Odstavek 3: predlogi
I would recommend advertising the event earlier and inviting local craftspeople, as we had to turn away people with broken electronics.
Predlog: I would recommend + -ing / It would be a good idea to …
Conclusion – Overall, the project was a success and should definitely be repeated.
Kratek sklep. Formalen jezik, brez skrajšanih oblik (don't → do not).
Točke se podelijo za vsebino (vse tri iztočnice), zgradbo in obliko (glava, odstavki), besedišče in slovnico. Preštej besede: 120–150.

naloge.besedilo:
Choose ONE essay title.

  1. Young people should spend a year volunteering before university.
  2. Cities should be designed for pedestrians, not cars.

Underline the essay title you have chosen. How far do you agree or disagree with the statement? Support your opinion in 220–250 words.
naloge.rezultat: Argumentativni esej z jasnim stališčem v uvodu, dvema ali tremi argumenti s primeri, upoštevanim protiargumentom in sklepom; 220–250 besed, en sam izbrani naslov.
naloge.razlaga:
Načrt (velja za oba naslova)
Uvod: preoblikuj trditev in jasno povej svoje stališče (I largely agree that …).
Ocenjevalci iščejo jasno tezo že v uvodu. Ne prepiši naslova dobesedno.
Jedro 1: prvi argument + primer (A gap year of volunteering teaches responsibility …).
Vsak odstavek ima temeljno poved, razlago in konkreten primer (izkušnja, podatek, primer iz Slovenije).
Jedro 2: drugi argument + primer (… it also helps students choose the right course).
Povezovalci: Furthermore, What is more, In addition.
Jedro 3: protiargument in zavrnitev (Critics argue that … However, …).
Upoštevanje nasprotnega mnenja pokaže zrelost argumentacije in prinese točke za vsebino.
Sklep: povzemi stališče brez novih argumentov (All things considered, …).
Sklep naj odgovori na vprašanje »How far do you agree?«.
Ideje za 2. naslov
For: cleaner air, safer streets, more local shops, healthier citizens. Against: older people and deliveries depend on cars, public transport is not always available.
Izberi le en naslov in ga podčrtaj. Nevtralen, formalen slog, brez skrajšanih oblik.

The Last Bookshop

Every town has a place where time behaves differently. In ours it was Maddox & Daughter, a bookshop squeezed between a bakery and a shoe repairer on Castle Street. The sign said "Est. 1923", although Mrs Maddox liked to tell customers that the date had been painted by her grandfather after a particularly good lunch and might not be entirely accurate.

I started working there at sixteen, on Saturdays, for a wage so small that Mrs Maddox paid it partly in books. She explained the arrangement as if it were a great privilege. "Money," she said, "goes into your pocket and disappears. A book goes into your head and stays." I did not argue. I was too busy being amazed that someone would pay me – even in paperbacks – to spend the day in a room that smelt of paper and dust and the cinnamon rolls from next door.

The shop had no computer. Mrs Maddox kept the stock in her memory and in a series of school exercise books, one for each letter of the alphabet, filled with her tiny, slanting handwriting. When a customer asked for a title, she would close her eyes for a moment, as though listening to a distant radio, and then walk directly to the right shelf. She was wrong so rarely that the regulars treated her mistakes as small public holidays.

It was not a profitable business. Most weeks, the shop earned just enough to pay the rent, and in bad months Mrs Maddox sold her own furniture, piece by piece. Her daughter, who lived in London and worked for an insurance company, phoned every Sunday to beg her to close. "Nobody buys books in shops any more, Mum," I once heard her say through the receiver, so loudly that I could hear every word from the back room.

Then, one February, a developer bought the whole row of buildings. The bakery accepted his offer at once. The shoe repairer held out for a month. Mrs Maddox simply ignored his letters, using the envelopes as bookmarks.

What happened next surprised everyone, including her. A girl from my school posted a photograph of the shop online with the words "Save the last bookshop". Within a week, there were queues on Castle Street. People who had not bought a book in years came to buy three. A retired lawyer offered to fight the developer for free.

The shop is still there. It has a computer now, which Mrs Maddox refuses to touch. "It keeps telling me what I already know," she complains, and goes on writing in her exercise books.

Accidental inventions that changed everyday life

Not every great invention was planned. Some of the most useful objects we own were discovered by mistake.

A The microwave oven

In 1945, the American engineer Percy Spencer was testing equipment for military radar when he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. Curious, he placed some popcorn kernels near the machine and watched them burst. The first commercial microwave oven was nearly two metres tall and weighed more than 300 kilograms, so it was sold only to restaurants and ships. It took another twenty years before a version small and cheap enough for ordinary kitchens appeared.

B Sticky notes

The scientist Spencer Silver was trying to create a super-strong glue in 1968, but he produced the opposite: an adhesive so weak that it could be removed without leaving a mark. For years nobody knew what to do with it. The solution came from his colleague Art Fry, who was tired of the paper bookmarks falling out of his hymn book at church. The company was not convinced at first, and early tests in shops failed because customers did not understand the product until they were given free samples.

C The pacemaker

In 1956, Wilson Greatbatch, an engineer working on a device to record heart sounds, reached into a box for a resistor and took the wrong one. When he switched the circuit on, it produced a regular electrical pulse that reminded him of a heartbeat. He immediately understood what it could mean for patients with heart problems. He spent two years in a barn behind his house developing a small device, and today millions of people live longer thanks to his mistake.

D Safety glass

One day in 1903, the French chemist Édouard Bénédictus knocked a glass flask off a shelf in his laboratory. To his surprise, it cracked but did not break into pieces. The flask had contained a plastic solution that had dried and formed a thin film on the inside. He did not think about it again until he read about drivers injured by broken windscreens. He then patented laminated glass, but car manufacturers showed little interest at first because it was expensive, and the material was first used widely in gas masks during the First World War.

E Super glue

During the Second World War, Harry Coover was trying to make clear plastic gun sights. One of the materials he tested stuck to everything it touched, and he rejected it as useless. Nine years later he came across the same substance again and realised that its stickiness was its value. Since then it has been used for everything from mending toys to closing wounds; during the Vietnam War medics used a spray version to stop bleeding on the battlefield.

Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Today we remember a woman whose name was almost forgotten for more than a century: Mary Anning, who was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the Dorset coast. Her family was poor. Her father, Richard, was a carpenter who earned a little extra money by selling curiosities – shells and strange stones – to tourists who came to the seaside in summer.

The cliffs around Lyme Regis are made of soft rock that slips into the sea after every storm, and with each landslide new fossils appear. Richard took Mary and her brother Joseph along the beach to collect them. When he died in 1810, he left the family in debt, and fossil hunting turned from a hobby into the family's main income.

In 1811, Joseph found a strange skull. Over the next months, Mary, who was only twelve, uncovered the rest of the skeleton. It was an ichthyosaur, a marine reptile, and it was the first complete one ever identified. Later she discovered the first plesiosaur skeleton, an animal with a tiny head and an extremely long neck. When the French scientist Georges Cuvier saw the drawings, he thought it must be a fake. A meeting of experts was called, and only after they had examined the bones did Cuvier admit that he had been wrong.

Mary had almost no formal education, but she taught herself geology and anatomy. She even dissected modern fish and cuttlefish to understand the animals she was digging up. Gentlemen scientists visited her shop to ask for her opinion, yet when they published papers about her finds, her name was usually missing. As a woman, she could not join the Geological Society of London, and she was not allowed to attend its meetings.

The work was dangerous. In 1833, a landslide killed her dog, Tray, only a few metres away from her. Mary carried on working until she died of breast cancer in 1847, at the age of forty-seven.

Today, her story is told in museums, in children's books and even in a feature film. In 2010, the Royal Society named her one of the ten British women who have most influenced the history of science, and in 2022 a statue of her was finally unveiled in Lyme Regis.

Mary Anning

You will hear an interview with Tom Blake, who keeps bees on the roofs of London. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Tom, you look after bees in the middle of London. How did that start?

Tom: By accident, really. I was working in an office in the City, and one day a swarm landed on the window of our meeting room. Nobody knew what to do, so I phoned a beekeeper, and I was fascinated by how calmly she collected them. Within a year I had done a course and had two hives on my own balcony.

Interviewer: And now?

Tom: Now I manage about sixty hives on the roofs of hotels, banks and a hospital. Companies pay me to keep the bees, and in return they get honey with their own label. Many of them use it as a present for clients.

Interviewer: Isn't a city a strange place for bees?

Tom: People think so, but London is full of parks, private gardens and railway embankments. There is a greater variety of flowers than in the countryside, where you often have huge fields of just one crop. That's why city honey usually tastes more complex – every jar is a mixture of hundreds of plants.

Interviewer: Is there a downside?

Tom: Yes, and it's an important one. There are now so many hives in central London that there isn't enough food for all the bees, especially in late summer. Honeybees then compete with wild bees, and wild bees lose. So I tell companies that are thinking of getting hives: plant flowers first. A roof garden helps more than another hive.

Interviewer: What does a typical day look like for you?

Tom: In spring I open every hive once a week to check that the queen is laying eggs and that the colony isn't preparing to swarm. A strong colony can have fifty thousand bees, and if they swarm from a hotel roof onto a busy street, you get calls from the police. The hardest part of the job is carrying equipment up the stairs – most of these buildings don't let you use the lifts.

Interviewer: Do you get stung?

Tom: All the time! About once a day in summer. You stop reacting after a while, although I always carry medicine in case a visitor is allergic.

Interviewer: Finally, what is the most important thing your bees have taught you?

Tom: Patience. You can't hurry bees. If you move fast, they get nervous. So I've learned to slow down, which, for someone who used to work in finance, is quite a change.

An interview with a beekeeper

The Allotment

My grandfather had three loves: my grandmother, the radio cricket commentary and Plot 47 at the Riverside Allotments. Not necessarily in that order, my grandmother used to say.

Plot 47 was a strip of land about the size of a tennis court, rented from the town council for twelve pounds a year. Grandad had taken it over in 1971 from a retired bus driver who left him a shed, a broken wheelbarrow and a single instruction written on the shed door in white paint: "Never plant mint in the open ground." It took Grandad two summers and a great deal of digging to understand why. Mint, it turns out, spreads underground like a rumour.

I started going with him when I was seven, mostly because the allotment had a tap, a hose and a great deal of mud, and nobody seemed to mind if I combined the three. Gradually, though, I began to understand that the place had its own society. There was Mrs Okafor, who grew vegetables nobody else could name and gave them away in brown paper bags. There was Mr Lewandowski, who measured his onions with a ruler and entered them in competitions. And there was a long-running disagreement between the plots on the river side and the plots on the road side, which had started over a shared water barrel in 1985 and had never been properly resolved.

Grandad believed that you could judge a person by the state of their compost heap. His own was a work of art, built in layers like a cake: green leaves, brown cardboard, kitchen scraps, a spade of soil. He turned it every Sunday with the seriousness of a priest.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandad's knees stopped cooperating. He could still sit in his folding chair by the shed and give instructions, but the digging became my job. I complained loudly and often. I was embarrassed when friends saw me cycling home with a bag of potatoes on the handlebars.

Then, in August, Mr Lewandowski fell ill a week before the town show, and Grandad sent me to water his onions. I measured them too, out of curiosity. The biggest was nineteen centimetres across. I entered it in his name, and it won second prize.

Grandad has been gone for four years now. I still rent Plot 47. The shed door still says "Never plant mint in the open ground." Underneath, in my own white paint, I have added: "Turn the compost on Sundays."

Five novels that still start arguments

Teachers love them, some parents fear them, and teenagers keep reading them. Here are five classics that regularly appear on school reading lists – and on lists of books that someone wants removed.

A To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee (1960)

Told through the eyes of Scout, a young girl in a small town in Alabama, the novel follows her father's attempt to defend a Black man accused of a crime he did not commit. It won the Pulitzer Prize and has sold more than forty million copies. Some schools have taken it off the curriculum because of the racist language used by several characters, while others argue that this language is exactly what makes the book an honest lesson about injustice.

B The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins (2008)

In a future North America, teenagers are forced to fight to the death on live television. Collins has said she got the idea while switching channels between a reality show and news from a war. Critics have complained that the book is too violent for young readers, yet many teachers use it to start discussions about the media, inequality and the way societies control people with entertainment.

C The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time by Mark Haddon (2003)

Fifteen-year-old Christopher, who is brilliant at maths but finds people confusing, decides to investigate the death of a neighbour's dog. The novel was praised for showing the world from an unusual point of view, and it became a hugely successful stage play. Haddon himself has said that he did not research the topic in depth and regrets that the book is sometimes treated as a guide to autism.

D Lord of the Flies by William Golding (1954)

A group of British schoolboys are stranded on an island after a plane crash and try to govern themselves, with terrible results. Golding, who had been a teacher, wrote the book partly as a reply to adventure stories in which shipwrecked boys behave like perfect gentlemen. It was rejected by more than twenty publishers before it was accepted, and it later helped him win the Nobel Prize.

E Wonder by R. J. Palacio (2012)

August Pullman, a boy born with a facial difference, goes to a normal school for the first time at the age of ten. Palacio wrote the novel after an incident in which her own young son reacted with fear to a girl with a similar condition. The book inspired a campaign against bullying called 'Choose Kind', and it is one of the few books on this list that almost nobody has tried to ban.

In the early hours of the seventh of September 1838, a young woman looked out of a lighthouse window on the Farne Islands, off the coast of Northumberland, and saw something that would change her life. Her name was Grace Darling, she was twenty-two years old, and she had spent almost her whole life on the islands, where her father, William, was the lighthouse keeper.

That night a terrible storm was blowing. A steamship called the Forfarshire, carrying around sixty passengers and crew from Hull to Dundee, had problems with its engines and was driven onto a group of rocks called Big Harcar. The ship broke in two, and the back half sank almost immediately. Grace spotted the wreck at about a quarter to five in the morning, and through a telescope she could make out a few people clinging to the rocks.

The sea was far too rough for the lifeboat from the mainland to set out, so Grace and her father decided to row out themselves in a small fishing boat. They took the longer, more sheltered route, almost a mile, to reach the rocks. William jumped onto the rocks to help the survivors, while Grace kept the boat steady in the waves. They rescued nine people in two trips: the first time they took five, including an injured man, back to the lighthouse, and two of the rescued crew then helped William row back for the rest.

When the story appeared in the newspapers, Grace became a celebrity almost overnight. Artists travelled to the islands to paint her portrait, people wrote poems and songs about her, and she received hundreds of letters, some of them asking for a lock of her hair. Even Queen Victoria sent her fifty pounds. Grace found the attention exhausting; she was a shy person and did not understand why so much fuss was made, since her father had done just as much.

Sadly, she did not enjoy her fame for long. In 1842, just four years after the rescue, she died of tuberculosis at the age of twenty-six. Today there is a museum dedicated to her in the village of Bamburgh, and her name is still used for lifeboats around the British coast.

I look at them and we discuss the case over a video call. It's not science fiction; most of it works on an ordinary smartphone with a decent internet connection.

Interviewer: How did it all begin?

Dr Hassan: When I was a medical student, I spent a summer volunteering at a clinic in the mountains of Nepal. There was one doctor for about twenty thousand people. I remember a young boy with a broken leg who had to be carried for two days to reach us. I promised myself then that I would find a way to help places like that, even if I couldn't be there in person.

Interviewer: What kind of cases do you deal with?

Dr Hassan: Mostly emergencies – injuries, burns, difficult births. Often the local doctor knows exactly what to do but needs a second opinion before taking a big decision, like whether to send a patient on a long journey to a hospital. Sometimes I simply confirm what they already think. That confidence can save a life.

Interviewer: Are there limits to what you can do?

Dr Hassan: Of course. I can't touch the patient, and a photograph doesn't show everything. The biggest problem, though, is electricity. In many clinics, the power goes off for hours every day, so we've started giving them solar chargers. A phone with an empty battery is no use to anyone.

Interviewer: You also train volunteers.

Dr Hassan: Yes, we now have about four hundred doctors in twenty countries who give their time for free. Before they start, they do an online course about working with different cultures – how to explain things politely, how to ask questions without making a colleague feel stupid. That part is just as important as the medicine.

Interviewer: What's your next goal?

Dr Hassan: We want to translate our training materials into more languages. At the moment they exist only in English and French, which excludes many of the people who need them most.

Nobody in the village of Upper Wendle could remember exactly when Old Tobias had fallen asleep, only that it had been a Tuesday, that it had been raining, and that he had gone into the woods to look for a lost goat.

He was found two days later under an oak tree, breathing peacefully, with the goat grazing beside him. They carried him home on a door, laid him on his bed, and waited for him to wake up. He did not. The doctor came from the market town, listened to his heart, shone a light into his eyes, and pronounced him perfectly healthy, "apart from the obvious". He prescribed fresh air and patience, charged a guinea, and left.

At first the village treated the matter as an inconvenience. Tobias was the only man who knew how to repair the church clock, and within a month it had stopped at twenty past three. His wife, Martha, took over his duties at the mill, and found – somewhat to her own surprise – that she was better at the accounts than he had ever been. The baker's boy was sent every morning with a bowl of soup, which Martha fed to the sleeping man with a spoon, and which he swallowed without opening his eyes.

Years passed. Children who had been born after Tobias fell asleep were taken to see him as a kind of local attraction, and a few brave ones were allowed to touch his beard, which by now reached his belt. A travelling scientist wrote an article about him for a London journal, describing him as "a living clock that has stopped". The vicar preached sermons about him as an example of the patience of God.

Twenty years after he had gone into the woods, Tobias opened his eyes, sat up and asked for his goat. He was, everyone agreed later, remarkably calm about the whole thing. He walked to the inn, where he failed to recognise anyone, and was mildly offended when nobody recognised him either. He spoke confidently about the price of wheat, which had tripled, and about the young king, who had been dead for eleven years.

What troubled him most was not that the world had changed, but that it had managed so well without him. The mill was prospering. The church clock had been replaced by a new one from Birmingham. And Martha, he discovered, had been running the parish council for a decade.

"You might have waited," he said to her.

Money mattered, too. For many women, writing was one of the very few respectable ways of earning an income. [4] Elizabeth Gaskell used her earnings to buy a house for her family, a purchase she kept secret from her husband until the deal was done.

Grace spotted the wreck at about a quarter to five in the morning, and through a telescope she could make out a few people clinging to the rocks.

The sea was far too rough for the lifeboat from the mainland to set out, so Grace and her father decided to row out themselves in a small fishing boat. Interviewer: Dr Hassan, you work in a London hospital, but you also help patients thousands of kilometres away. How does that work?

Dr Hassan: Through a very simple system. Doctors in remote clinics – in mountain villages, on small islands, sometimes in places affected by war – send me photographs, X-rays and short videos on their mobile phones. I look at them and we discuss the case over a video call. It's not science fiction; most of it works on an ordinary smartphone with a decent internet connection.

Interviewer: How did it all begin?

Dr Hassan: When I was a medical student, I spent a summer volunteering at a clinic in the mountains of Nepal. There was one doctor for about twenty thousand people. I remember a young boy with a broken leg who had to be carried for two days to reach us. I promised myself then that I would find a way to help places like that, even if I couldn't be there in person.

Interviewer: What kind of cases do you deal with?

Dr Hassan: Mostly emergencies – injuries, burns, difficult births. Often the local doctor knows exactly what to do but needs a second opinion before taking a big decision, like whether to send a patient on a long journey to a hospital. Sometimes I simply confirm what they already think. That confidence can save a life.

Interviewer: Are there limits to what you can do?

Dr Hassan: Of course. I can't touch the patient, and a photograph doesn't show everything. The biggest problem, though, is electricity. In many clinics, the power goes off for hours every day, so we've started giving them solar chargers. A phone with an empty battery is no use to anyone.

Interviewer: You also train volunteers.

Dr Hassan: Yes, we now have about four hundred doctors in twenty countries who give their time for free. Before they start, they do an online course about working with different cultures – how to explain things politely, how to ask questions without making a colleague feel stupid. That part is just as important as the medicine.

Interviewer: What's your next goal?

Dr Hassan: We want to translate our training materials into more languages. At the moment they exist only in English and French, which excludes many of the people who need them most.

That was how my children discovered the classics – and how I discovered that "old" is not the same as "boring".

The first film we tried was a black-and-white comedy from the 1950s. My son, then eight, complained for the first ten minutes that "the colours were broken". By the end he was laughing so hard that he slid off his chair. What won him over was not the story but the physical comedy: people falling into rivers, getting stuck in doors, being chased by geese. Older films also move at a different speed. There are fewer cuts and longer scenes, which at first my daughter found frustrating. Slow films, I have come to believe, train children to pay attention.

Interviewer: Anna, you hold a world record for swimming under ice without breathing equipment. How far did you swim?

Anna: Ninety-five metres, in a lake in northern Norway, on a single breath. The water was about two degrees, and the ice above me was half a metre thick. I wore only a swimsuit, goggles and a hat.

Interviewer: Why no wetsuit?

Anna: For this record the rules don't allow one. Many people think that's crazy, but the body is surprisingly well designed for cold. In the first seconds your heart rate drops and the blood moves away from your arms and legs towards the organs that matter most. It's called the diving reflex, and every human has it, even babies.

Interviewer: How did you get into this sport?

Anna: I grew up on a farm next to a lake, and my grandmother swam in it every morning, all year round. When I was twelve she took me with her in January. I screamed, but I was hooked. I didn't start free diving seriously until I was thirty, after a difficult divorce. I needed something that made my mind completely quiet.

Interviewer: Is it dangerous?

Anna: Very, if you're careless. Under ice you can't simply come up for air – you have to find the hole you went in through. So we drill a second hole every twenty-five metres in case something goes wrong, and I'm connected to a safety line. I have a team of six divers and a doctor with me. The cold isn't the biggest risk. Panic is.

Interviewer: How do you train?

Anna: Mostly in a normal swimming pool, and on land. I do yoga and breathing exercises, and I spend a lot of time in cold showers. Mental training is half the work. Before a dive I imagine every metre, every stroke, until it feels like something I've already done.

Interviewer: What's next?

Anna: I want to use the attention to talk about climate change. The lakes where I train used to freeze in November. Now we sometimes wait until January. In twenty years, there may not be enough ice for this sport at all.

Interviewer: Dr Torres, you've spent fifteen years watching chimpanzees in Uganda. What were you looking for?

Dr Torres: Gestures. Chimpanzees use their voices, of course, but they also use their hands, faces and bodies to send very specific messages. We've now recorded more than seventy different gestures, and we're still finding new ones.

Interviewer: How do you study animals that live high in the trees?

Dr Torres: With enormous patience. The first rule is to behave as boringly as possible. If you're quiet and predictable, after a few months the chimps stop paying attention to you, and that's when they show you their real lives. I spend most days sitting on the ground with a video camera and a notebook, often for ten hours at a time.

Interviewer: Can you give an example of a gesture?

Dr Torres: One of my favourites is a gentle touch on the back of another chimp's hand. It means 'let's go' – a mother uses it with her baby when she wants to move on. Another is a loud slap on the ground, which is a way of saying 'stop that' or 'go away'. What's fascinating is that the meanings seem to be the same in different groups that have never met.

Interviewer: Does that tell us something about human language?

Dr Torres: We think it might. Babies point and wave long before they can speak, and many of their gestures look very similar to those of young chimps. One study even found that adults could guess the meaning of chimpanzee gestures from videos more often than chance would predict. That suggests that our ancestors may have communicated with their hands before they used words.

Interviewer: What are the biggest threats to the chimps you study?

Dr Torres: Loss of forest, mainly to farming, and diseases that humans pass on to them – a simple cold can kill a chimpanzee. That's why researchers in our project wear masks and keep a distance of at least seven metres.

The Collector

Mr Ferris collected things that other people threw away. Not rubbish, exactly – he was very particular about that – but objects that had lost their purpose: keys without locks, single gloves, maps of towns that had since changed their names. He kept them in labelled boxes in the attic of the narrow house on Pell Street, where he had lived alone since his sister's death.

I was eleven when I began to visit him, officially to deliver the newspaper, unofficially because he paid me in stories. Each week he would choose an object from a box and tell me where it had come from. A brass key had belonged to a lighthouse in Cornwall. A child's shoe had been found in the ruins of a bombed theatre. A ticket for a train that no longer ran had been bought, he said, by a woman who never used it, because the man she was meant to meet had changed his mind.

I believed every word. It was only years later, sorting through the boxes after his funeral, that I found the notebooks. In them, in his small, careful handwriting, were the stories – each one drafted, crossed out and rewritten several times. Some objects had three or four different histories. The brass key had once belonged to a prison, then to a castle, before he finally settled on the lighthouse.

My first reaction was anger, as if I had been cheated of something. My mother, who had never liked my visits to Pell Street, said that she had always known the old man was "a bit of a fantasist". But the anger did not last. Reading the notebooks, I began to understand what he had been doing. He had not been lying to me; he had been practising. Every week he had tested a story on his only audience, watched my face, and gone back to his desk to improve it.

He never published anything. As far as I know, he never showed the notebooks to anyone. Perhaps he did not think they were good enough. Perhaps he was simply happy to have one listener who wanted to hear the next chapter.

I kept the brass key. It sits on my desk now, beside the laptop on which I write my own stories. When I get stuck, I pick it up and ask it where it has been. It always has an answer, though rarely the same one twice.

Board games are enjoying a golden age. Here are five very different games for very different players.

A Moonfall

Moonfall is a co-operative game in which all players work together to save a space station from a falling moon. There is no single winner: either everybody survives or nobody does. The rules take about an hour to learn, and the first game can feel slow, but experienced players love the way every decision affects later ones. There is very little direct conflict, which makes it a good introduction for people who dislike games where you attack each other. Interviewer: Anna, you hold a world record for swimming under ice without breathing equipment. How far did you swim?

Anna: Ninety-five metres, in a lake in northern Norway, on a single breath. The water was about two degrees, and the ice above me was half a metre thick. I wore only a swimsuit, goggles and a hat.

Interviewer: Why no wetsuit?

Anna: For this record the rules don't allow one. Many people think that's crazy, but the body is surprisingly well designed for cold. In the first seconds your heart rate drops and the blood moves away from your arms and legs towards the organs that matter most. It's called the diving reflex, and every human has it, even babies.

Interviewer: How did you get into this sport?

Anna: I grew up on a farm next to a lake, and my grandmother swam in it every morning, all year round. When I was twelve she took me with her in January. I screamed, but I was hooked. I didn't start free diving seriously until I was thirty, after a difficult divorce. I needed something that made my mind completely quiet.

Interviewer: Is it dangerous?

Anna: Very, if you're careless. Under ice you can't simply come up for air – you have to find the hole you went in through. So we drill a second hole every twenty-five metres in case something goes wrong, and I'm connected to a safety line. I have a team of six divers and a doctor with me. The cold isn't the biggest risk. Panic is.

Interviewer: How do you train?

Anna: Mostly in a normal swimming pool, and on land. I do yoga and breathing exercises, and I spend a lot of time in cold showers. Mental training is half the work. Before a dive I imagine every metre, every stroke, until it feels like something I've already done.

Interviewer: What's next?

Anna: I want to use the attention to talk about climate change. The lakes where I train used to freeze in November. Now we sometimes wait until January. In twenty years, there may not be enough ice for this sport at all.

Interviewer: Dr Torres, you've spent fifteen years watching chimpanzees in Uganda. What were you looking for?

Dr Torres: Gestures. Chimpanzees use their voices, of course, but they also use their hands, faces and bodies to send very specific messages. We've now recorded more than seventy different gestures, and we're still finding new ones.

Interviewer: How do you study animals that live high in the trees?

Dr Torres: With enormous patience. The first rule is to behave as boringly as possible. If you're quiet and predictable, after a few months the chimps stop paying attention to you, and that's when they show you their real lives. I spend most days sitting on the ground with a video camera and a notebook, often for ten hours at a time.

Interviewer: Can you give an example of a gesture?

Dr Torres: One of my favourites is a gentle touch on the back of another chimp's hand. It means 'let's go' – a mother uses it with her baby when she wants to move on. Another is a loud slap on the ground, which is a way of saying 'stop that' or 'go away'. What's fascinating is that the meanings seem to be the same in different groups that have never met.

Interviewer: Does that tell us something about human language?

Dr Torres: We think it might. Babies point and wave long before they can speak, and many of their gestures look very similar to those of young chimps. One study even found that adults could guess the meaning of chimpanzee gestures from videos more often than chance would predict. That suggests that our ancestors may have communicated with their hands before they used words.

Interviewer: What are the biggest threats to the chimps you study?

Dr Torres: Loss of forest, mainly to farming, and diseases that humans pass on to them – a simple cold can kill a chimpanzee. That's why researchers in our project wear masks and keep a distance of at least seven metres.

Twenty Years: a documentary about waiting

How long can a family wait for someone? In the remarkable documentary Twenty Years, director Ana Ruiz follows a woman from Texas, Denise Carter, whose husband was sentenced to twenty years in prison for his part in a robbery in which nobody was hurt. Denise was twenty-four at the time, with two small sons and no job.

The film is built almost entirely from home videos. Denise started recording messages for her husband on a cheap camera the week he went to prison, so that he would not miss his sons growing up. Over two decades she filled more than three hundred tapes: birthday parties, first days at school, a broken arm, a graduation. Ruiz found the tapes by chance, when Denise mentioned them during a radio interview, and spent four years editing them.

What makes the film so powerful is that it is not only about prison. It is about the strange, stretched kind of time that families live in when someone is missing. In the early tapes, Denise is angry and frightened. Later she is tired, then determined. She goes back to college, becomes a teacher and starts a campaign for shorter sentences for non-violent crimes.

Her sons, Marcus and Jay, are perhaps the film's real heroes. As children, they speak to the camera as if their father were in the room. As teenagers, they refuse to record anything at all. One of the most moving scenes shows Jay, aged sixteen, finally sitting down in front of the camera and saying nothing for almost a minute before he begins to cry.

The film does not ask us to feel sorry for the father. He made a terrible mistake, and he says so. What it asks is whether a punishment that lasts twenty years punishes only the person who committed the crime. Ruiz never answers the question directly. Instead, she lets the tapes speak.

The ending, when the father is finally released, is shown without music. He walks out of the gate, looks at two grown men he hardly recognises, and asks if he can hold the camera. It is one of the most powerful final scenes I have seen in years.

Dan: Pigeons have lived alongside humans for at least five thousand years. They were probably the first birds to be domesticated, kept for their meat and for their droppings, which made an excellent fertiliser. Their most famous skill, of course, is finding their way home. In both world wars, pigeons carried messages across the battlefield, and one of them, a bird called Cher Ami, saved almost two hundred soldiers in 1918.

Dr Ellis: What fascinates me is how they navigate. We know they use the position of the sun, and they seem to be able to sense the Earth's magnetic field. But recent studies suggest they also follow human roads. Pigeons tracked with GPS often fly along motorways and even turn at roundabouts.

Dan: Dr Sarah Ellis studies pigeons at a university in Oxford. Her research has shown that the birds can recognise individual human faces.

Dan: Pigeons can also learn to tell the difference between paintings by Monet and Picasso, and they can count up to nine. So why do we dislike them so much?

City pigeons are descended from birds that escaped from farms, and they survive on the food we throw away. If we stopped feeding them, their numbers would fall naturally within a few years.

Dan: Some cities are trying a gentler solution: special pigeon lofts where the birds are encouraged to nest, and where their eggs are replaced with plastic ones. In Basel, in Switzerland, the population has been halved this way, without a single bird being killed.

The Telegram

Knowing that Mrs Hale had a weak heart, the family took great care to tell her the news as gently as possible. It was her sister Clara who did it, in broken sentences and half-finished hints, while Mr Hale's old friend Robert waited in the hall. He had been at the newspaper office when the telegram arrived, listing the names of those lost in the railway accident, and Brently Hale's name had been at the top.

Mrs Hale did not react as other women might have done, unable to accept the truth. She wept at once, suddenly and wildly, in her sister's arms. When the first storm of grief was over, she went to her room alone. She would have no one follow her.

There, facing the open window, stood a comfortable armchair. She sank into it, exhausted. Outside, the tops of the trees were trembling with new spring life. The smell of rain was in the air. In the street below a man was selling vegetables, and somewhere a voice was singing. Sparrows were arguing on the roof.

She sat quite still, except when a sob came up into her throat and shook her, like a child who has cried itself to sleep and continues to sob in its dreams. She was young, with a calm face whose lines showed a certain strength.

Something was coming to her, and she was waiting for it, fearfully. What was it? She did not know; it was too subtle to name. But she felt it creeping out of the sky, through the sounds and the colours that filled the air.

When she let it come, a little whispered word escaped from her lips. She said it over and over: "Free, free, free!" The empty stare and the look of terror went from her eyes. Her pulse beat fast, and her blood warmed every part of her body.

She knew that she would weep again when she saw his kind hands folded in death. But beyond that bitter moment she saw a long procession of years that would belong to her absolutely. There would be no one to live for during those coming years; she would live for herself.

Clara was kneeling at the closed door, begging her to come out. "You will make yourself ill," she said. But Mrs Hale was drinking in the very air of life through that open window.

At last she rose and opened the door. There was a feverish triumph in her eyes, and she carried herself unconsciously like a goddess of victory. Someone was opening the front door with a key. It was Brently Hale who entered, a little dusty, carrying his bag and umbrella. He had been far from the scene of the accident and did not even know there had been one.

When the doctors came, they said she had died of heart disease – of joy that kills.

A billion users can't all be wrong

Many people still think of TikTok as an app for dance videos. [0] For millions of young people, it has become a place to learn, to find a community and, increasingly, to get the news.

When politicians discuss the platform, they usually focus on two issues: data security and the effect of short videos on attention spans. [1] What they rarely discuss is why so many people use the app in the first place.

The answer, according to researchers, is the algorithm. Unlike older social networks, TikTok does not depend mainly on who you follow. [2] As a result, an unknown creator can reach millions of viewers with a single video.

This has changed who gets heard. [3] A nurse explaining a medical procedure, a farmer showing how cheese is made, a teenager talking about living with a disability – all of them can find an audience without the help of a television channel or a publisher.

Of course, the same system can spread false information just as quickly. [4] Fact-checkers say they cannot keep up with the speed at which misleading videos go viral.

Young users are not as naïve as adults often assume, however. [5] Many say they check information they see on TikTok against other sources, and that they treat the app as a starting point rather than an authority.

There is also a question of fairness. [6] If the platform were banned, they argue, millions of small businesses that sell products through the app would lose an important source of income.

Supporters of tighter regulation reply that this is precisely why rules are needed. [7] They call for more transparency about how the algorithm works and stronger protection for children.

Perhaps the real lesson is that politicians need to understand the platforms they want to control. [8] Until they do, they risk making decisions that a billion users will simply ignore. [9]

Presenter: They're everywhere – on statues, railway stations and café tables – and most of us see them as pests. But pigeons have a surprisingly rich history, and scientists are discovering that they're much cleverer than we think. Our reporter, Dan Moss, has been finding out more.

Dan: Pigeons have lived alongside humans for at least five thousand years. They were probably the first birds to be domesticated, kept for their meat and for their droppings, which made an excellent fertiliser. Their most famous skill, of course, is finding their way home. In both world wars, pigeons carried messages across the battlefield, and one of them, a bird called Cher Ami, saved almost two hundred soldiers in 1918.

Dr Ellis: What fascinates me is how they navigate. We know they use the position of the sun, and they seem to be able to sense the Earth's magnetic field. But recent studies suggest they also follow human roads. Pigeons tracked with GPS often fly along motorways and even turn at roundabouts.

Dan: Dr Sarah Ellis studies pigeons at a university in Oxford. Her research has shown that the birds can recognise individual human faces.

Dr Ellis: In one experiment, two researchers fed pigeons in a park. One was friendly, the other chased the birds away. After a few days they swapped coats, but the pigeons still avoided the unfriendly one. They weren't fooled by clothes – they remembered the face.

Dan: Pigeons can also learn to tell the difference between paintings by Monet and Picasso, and they can count up to nine. So why do we dislike them so much?

Dr Ellis: Partly because there are so many of them, and partly because of their droppings, which damage buildings. But the real problem is us. City pigeons are descended from birds that escaped from farms, and they survive on the food we throw away. If we stopped feeding them, their numbers would fall naturally within a few years.

Dan: Some cities are trying a gentler solution: special pigeon lofts where the birds are encouraged to nest, and where their eggs are replaced with plastic ones. In Basel, in Switzerland, the population has been halved this way, without a single bird being killed.

The hidden lives of pigeons

The Pre-Party

As soon as the date for the school leavers' ball was announced, Martin's father, Greg, decided to host the "pre-party". He was not asked. He simply announced it at dinner, with the confidence of a man who had already ordered the balloons.

"Your mum and I will do canapés," he said. "Champagne for the parents, something fizzy and non-alcoholic for you lot. Photos in the garden. The roses will be out by then."

Martin, who was seventeen and had been hoping to arrive at the ball quietly with his two best friends, put down his fork. "Nobody does pre-parties any more, Dad."

"Everybody does pre-parties," said Greg. "Ask Sophie's mother."

It turned out that Sophie's mother had been planning her own pre-party for months, and that she regarded Greg's announcement as a declaration of war. Within a week, the school's parent group had divided into two camps. Messages flew. Some families accepted both invitations and spent anxious evenings working out how to be at two houses at the same time. Others accepted neither and said they would "see how things go", which everyone understood to mean that they were waiting to see which party had the better food.

Martin's mother, Helen, tried to stay out of it. She had been through the same thing when Martin's older sister left school, and she knew that the excitement of parents was always greater than the excitement of their children. But even she could not resist redesigning the garden. She bought new lights for the apple tree and spent a weekend painting the fence a colour called "Seaside Mist".

The night before the ball, it began to rain. It rained all night and all morning, and by lunchtime the garden was a small lake. The roses had been flattened. Greg stood at the kitchen window for an hour without speaking.

At four o'clock, the phone rang. It was Sophie's mother. Her marquee had collapsed in the wind, and she wondered – rather stiffly – whether the two parties might be combined, indoors, at Greg's house, which was bigger.

That evening, forty teenagers and sixty parents squeezed into the living room, the hall and the kitchen. Someone's grandmother played the piano. The photographs, taken on the stairs, were the best anybody could remember. And Martin, to his own surprise, did not want to leave.

Five children's authors who weren't afraid of the dark

Fairy tales were never meant to be comfortable. These five writers knew that children can handle more than adults think.

A Hans Christian Andersen

The Danish writer's stories are full of suffering: a little mermaid who feels as if she is walking on knives, a match girl who freezes to death on New Year's Eve. Andersen grew up in poverty, and he never forgot it. Although he became famous across Europe and was received by kings, he remained convinced all his life that he was an outsider, and many of his heroes share that feeling.

B The Brothers Grimm

Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm did not invent their stories – they collected them from storytellers, many of them women from middle-class families. The first edition of their collection, published in 1812, was criticised for being too violent and not suitable for children, so later editions were rewritten. Ironically, the brothers removed some of the sexual content but added even more violence.

C Roald Dahl

Dahl's books are packed with cruel adults who get what they deserve. He worked as a fighter pilot in the Second World War and suffered serious head injuries in a crash, an experience that some biographers believe influenced his dark sense of humour. In 2023 his publisher changed hundreds of words in his books, a decision that caused a huge public argument and led to the original versions being republished.

D Neil Gaiman

Gaiman's novel Coraline tells the story of a girl who discovers a door to another world, where a woman with buttons for eyes wants to keep her forever. Many adults found the book terrifying, but Gaiman noticed that children usually read it as an adventure. He wrote it, he says, for his own daughter, who complained that there were not enough scary stories for girls.

E Lemony Snicket

Behind the pen name Lemony Snicket is the American writer Daniel Handler. His thirteen-book series about three orphans warns readers on the very first page that the story will not have a happy ending. Handler has said that he was inspired by the frustration he felt as a child with books in which everything turned out fine. The series has been adapted for film and television.

I got my nickname, 'Sparrow', at school in Dublin, because I was the smallest boy in the class and I never stopped singing. I hated it at first. Now it's on the cover of every album, so I suppose I've made my peace with it.

We started the band forty years ago in my parents' garage. There were four of us, all fifteen, and only one of us could actually play an instrument. Our first concert was at a school disco, and we were so nervous that we played the same song three times because we'd forgotten the others. Somehow, people danced anyway.

It's strange, but the four of us are still together. People often ask how we've managed it, and the honest answer is that we never let money divide us. From the very first day, everything has been split equally – four ways – no matter who wrote the song. That has saved us from a lot of arguments.

My mother died when I was fourteen, and I think that's really why I started writing songs. I didn't know how to talk about what I felt, so I wrote it down instead. Many of our most famous songs are, if you listen carefully, about loss.

Over the years I've used our success to support causes I care about, especially the fight against poverty in Africa. I've met presidents and prime ministers, and I'm sometimes criticised for that. People say a rock star should stick to music. But if a politician will listen to me for ten minutes because I'm famous, I think I'd be foolish not to use those ten minutes.

These days I still write every morning, usually before anyone else in the house is awake. I'm not as fast as I used to be. But I've learned that the best songs often come when you stop trying so hard.

Presenter: Today I'm talking to the historian Dr Laura Finch, whose new book tells the story of Harold Gillies, the man often called the father of modern plastic surgery. Laura, why did you want to write about him?

Dr Finch: Simply because it's a wonderful story. Gillies was a New Zealander who came to England to study medicine and ended up working as an ear, nose and throat surgeon. When the First World War began, he volunteered for the Red Cross and was sent to France.

Presenter: And that changed his career?

Twenty years ago, the night train seemed to be dying. Today, the night train is back – and in some places, tickets sell out months in advance.

The revival began in 2016, when Austrian Railways took over several routes that German Railways had decided to close. Many experts thought the decision was a mistake. Instead, passenger numbers grew so quickly that the company ordered a new generation of trains, with private cabins that include their own shower and toilet.

The main reason for the change is climate. A journey by night train produces up to ten times less carbon dioxide than the same journey by plane. Still, governments are beginning to listen. Why schools should teach students how to fail

Most of us are afraid of failure. At school, a bad mark can feel like a disaster, and many students would rather not try at all than risk getting something wrong. [0] Yet psychologists say that learning to deal with failure may be one of the most important skills a young person can have.

The idea is not new. [1] Thomas Edison is said to have tested thousands of materials before he found one that worked in his light bulb.

Some schools are now trying to put this idea into practice. [2] In one London school, pupils take part in a "failure week", during which teachers talk openly about their own mistakes.

The results have been surprising. [3] Students who had previously avoided difficult questions began to put their hands up more often.

Researchers explain this with the idea of a "growth mindset". [4] People who believe that intelligence is fixed tend to give up quickly, while those who believe it can grow see mistakes as information.

Not everyone is convinced, however. [5] Some critics argue that celebrating failure sends the wrong message and that students still need to know when work is not good enough.

Parents, too, play an important role. [6] Children who are always protected from disappointment may find it harder to cope when things go wrong later in life.

The key, experts say, is how adults react. [7] Praising effort and strategy, rather than talent, teaches children that they can improve.

Of course, failure is never pleasant. [8] But it is often the moment when real learning begins.

As one teacher puts it, "If my students never make mistakes, the work is too easy." [9] Perhaps, then, the most useful lesson a school can teach is how to get up again. [10]

Interviewer: Dr Shah, what exactly is a tiny forest?

Dr Shah: It's a very dense forest about the size of a tennis court. The method comes from a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki, who developed it in the 1970s. Instead of planting a few trees far apart, you plant around six hundred young trees very close together – three per square metre.

Interviewer: Why so close?

Dr Shah: Because the trees compete for light, so they grow upwards very fast – about ten times faster than in a normal plantation. After three years the forest needs no more care at all. We also use only native species, at least thirty different ones, so the forest is similar to the one that would have grown there naturally.

Interviewer: What are the benefits in a city?

Dr Shah: Many. A tiny forest can be several degrees cooler than the street next to it on a hot day. It absorbs rainwater, reduces noise and attracts wildlife. In our first forest in Leeds, volunteers counted over five hundred species of insects and animals within two years.

Interviewer: Who does the planting?

Dr Shah: Local people, especially schoolchildren. A planting day usually takes a single morning. We think it's important that people feel the forest belongs to them, so each forest has a group of "tree keepers" from the neighbourhood who collect data and organise events.

Interviewer: Are there any critics?

Dr Shah: Yes. Some foresters say the method is expensive, and that not all the trees will survive in such crowded conditions. That's true – some will die. But that is exactly what happens in a natural forest too.

E-mail

Two months ago you joined a fitness club in your town. The advertisement promised modern equipment, small groups and personal advice from a qualified trainer. Unfortunately, you are not satisfied with the club.

Write an e-mail of complaint of 120–150 words to the club's manager, in which you:

  • explain two problems you have had and give an example for each of them,
  • say what you expect the club to do.
TO: manager@fitclub.si
SUBJECT: Complaint
Dear Sir or Madam,
naloge.rezultat: Formalna pritožba z namenom, dvema težavama (vsaka s primerom, primerjava z obljubami oglasa) in jasnim pričakovanjem (popravilo, nadomestilo); 120–150 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Zgradba pritožbe
Dear Sir or Madam,
Formalni nagovor (ime ni znano).
I am writing to complain about the service at your fitness club, which I joined two months ago.
Namen v prvem stavku.
Firstly, although your advertisement promised small groups, there are often more than thirty people in my evening class, so the trainer cannot correct our exercises.
1. težava + primer; primerjava z oglasom.
Secondly, two of the running machines have been out of order for over three weeks, and nobody has repaired them.
2. težava + konkreten primer.
I would therefore expect you to repair the equipment as soon as possible and to offer me a month's free membership as compensation.
Pričakovanje – vljudno, a odločno.
I look forward to your prompt reply. Yours faithfully, Dominik(a) Novak
Formalni zaključek.

naloge.besedilo:
Choose ONE essay title.

  1. Travelling teaches us more than school does.
  2. Social media is changing friendship for the worse.

Underline the essay title you have chosen. How far do you agree or disagree with the statement? Support your opinion in 220–250 words.

naloge.razlaga:
Načrt
Uvod: stališče (I partly agree: travel teaches lessons that school cannot, but it cannot replace school).
Jasna teza že v uvodu.
Argument 1: travel teaches independence and problem-solving, e.g. finding your way in a foreign city without help.
Argument + konkreten primer.
Argument 2: meeting other cultures builds tolerance and improves language skills.
Povezovalci: Moreover, In addition.
Protiargument: school gives systematic knowledge and is available to everyone, while travel is expensive.
However, … – upoštevaj drugo stran.
Sklep: the two complement each other.
Sklep odgovori na naslov.
Ideje za 2. naslov
For: fewer face-to-face meetings, likes instead of real support. Against: easier to stay in touch with friends abroad.
Izberi en naslov.

The Lodger

The lodger arrived on the first Monday of October, carrying a single suitcase and a cello case that was almost as tall as he was. My mother had put a card in the newsagent's window – ROOM TO LET, QUIET PERSON PREFERRED – and I think she regretted the word "quiet" the moment she saw the cello.

His name was Mr Adler, and he was older than she had expected, with white hair and a coat that had once been expensive. He paid three months' rent in cash, in advance, which was more money than I had ever seen on our kitchen table. My mother counted it twice and then hid it in the biscuit tin.

For the first week we hardly heard him. He left the house at seven every morning and came back after dark. Then, on Saturday afternoon, the music began. It came through the ceiling of my bedroom, slow and deep, and I sat on the floor with my back against the wall and did not move until it stopped. I was twelve, and I had never heard anything like it.

After that I began to wait for Saturdays. Sometimes he played the same short passage again and again, as if he were trying to find something he had lost. My mother complained that it gave her a headache, but I noticed she stopped hoovering whenever he started.

In December, Mr Adler fell ill. My mother took him soup and, because he could not climb the stairs to the bathroom, she moved him into our front room. That was when I learned that he had played in an orchestra in Vienna, that he had left in a hurry many years before, and that he had not spoken to his brother since.

He recovered by the spring, and in April he told us he was leaving. A letter had come from Vienna. On his last evening he played for us in the front room, with the curtains open, and people stopped in the street to listen. The next morning his room was empty, except for an envelope addressed to me. Inside was a ticket for a concert, and a note: "For the girl who listens through walls."

(Vadbeno besedilo Piflar.si)

  4. 3.Where did the mother keep the rent money?
  5. 4.When did Mr Adler first play the cello in the house?
  6. 5.How did the narrator react to the music the first time?
  7. 6.What did Mr Adler's repetition of a passage seem like to the narrator?
  8. 7.What shows that the mother secretly liked the music?
  9. 8.Why was Mr Adler moved into the front room?
  10. 9.Who had Mr Adler not spoken to for many years?
  11. 10.What did Mr Adler leave for the narrator?
