The psychology of keeping things

Almost everyone has a drawer full of objects they never use but cannot throw away: old concert tickets, a broken watch, a stone from a beach. [0] Psychologists have long been interested in why we hold on to such things.

Part of the answer lies in memory. [1] An old ticket can bring back an entire evening – the music, the weather, the people we were with.

Objects can also help us feel connected to people we have lost. [2] For many, a parent's handwriting on a birthday card is more precious than any expensive gift.

Interestingly, the attachment often begins in early childhood. [3] Around the age of two, many children choose a blanket or a soft toy that comforts them when their parents are not there.

In one famous experiment, researchers offered young children an identical copy of their favourite toy. [4] Most refused to swap, even though the copy was, in every way, the same.

Adults behave in a similar way. [5] Economists call this the "endowment effect": once something is ours, we value it more highly than before.

For some people, however, keeping things becomes a serious problem. [6] Their homes fill up until there is no room to cook, sleep or move safely.

Therapists who work with such people do not simply tell them to throw everything away. [7] Instead, they help them understand what each object represents, and find other ways of keeping the memory alive.

Some families have found their own solutions. [8] One woman photographed every object in her late father's workshop before giving the tools to a local school.

In the end, perhaps what we keep says less about the objects themselves than about who we are. [9] A drawer of "useless" things may, in fact, be a kind of autobiography. [10]

  2. BEach of these objects carries a story.
  3. CThat approach usually makes the anxiety worse.
  4. DThey believed that the original had something the copy lacked.
  5. EA familiar object can act as a key that opens the door to the past.
  6. FPsychologists call these 'transitional objects'.
  7. GThis condition, known as hoarding disorder, affects around two per cent of adults.
  8. HInstead of keeping the things, they keep a record of them.
  9. IClothes that still smell of someone, for instance, can be impossible to give away.
  10. JThey tell the story of what we have loved and lost.
  11. KAnd, unlike a diary, nobody else can read it.
  12. LChildren usually lose interest in their toys by the age of five.
  13. MMost people throw away the majority of their possessions every few years.

The island where people talk by whistling

On La Gomera, one of the smaller Canary Islands, you may hear something strange as you walk through the mountains: two people having a conversation (0) a single spoken word. They are using Silbo Gomero, a language (1) consists entirely of whistles.

The island is full of deep valleys, and walking from one village to the next can take hours. Whistling, (2) the other hand, can be heard up to five kilometres away. For centuries, shepherds and farmers used it to pass on news, warn of danger and arrange meetings (3) having to leave their fields.

Silbo is not a code but a way of whistling Spanish. Speakers replace vowels and consonants (4) changes in pitch and length, and listeners who know the language can understand (5) is being said almost as easily as normal speech.

In the second half of the twentieth century, the language nearly disappeared. Roads and telephones made it less necessary, and many young people moved away (6) search of work. By the 1980s, only a few elderly speakers were left, and linguists feared that within a generation it would be lost (7) ever.

The turning point came in 1999, (8) the local government made Silbo a compulsory subject in island schools. Today every child on La Gomera learns it for at (9) two years, and in 2009 UNESCO added it to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

Scientists have become interested (10) well. Brain scans show that experienced whistlers process Silbo in the same areas of the brain that are used for spoken language, (11) suggests that the brain treats it as real language rather than as music.

Not everyone is optimistic about the future. Although children learn the language at school, few of them use it in everyday life, (12) there are fewer and fewer reasons to whistle across a valley. Gone without a word: the rise of ghosting

It happens to almost everyone sooner or later. You have been chatting with someone for weeks, and then, (0) (SUDDEN), they stop answering. No explanation, no goodbye – just silence. The practice has become so common that it has its own name: ghosting.

Although the word is new, the behaviour is not. People have always found ways to avoid (1) (PLEASANT) conversations. What has changed is how easy it has become. When most of our (2) (RELATION) are carried on through screens, ending one requires nothing more than ignoring a (3) (NOTIFY).

For the person who is ghosted, the experience can be surprisingly painful. Psychologists say that the lack of an (4) (EXPLAIN) is the worst part: without one, people tend to blame themselves and go over every message, looking for a mistake. Some describe a feeling of (5) (HELP), because they have no chance to respond.

Why do people ghost? Surveys suggest that most do it not out of (6) (CRUEL) but to avoid conflict. Many say they did not want to hurt the other person, or simply did not know what to say. Others admit that the relationship was so (7) (SIGNIFY) to them that they did not think an ending was necessary.

Ghosting is not limited to romance. Friends drift apart in the same way, and even employers have been accused of ghosting job (8) (APPLY) after several rounds of interviews. Interestingly, the opposite also happens: (9) (INCREASE) numbers of new employees accept a job offer and then never turn up on their first day.

Experts disagree about how serious the problem is. Some see ghosting as a sign of a wider (10) (WILLING) to deal with difficult emotions, made worse by technology. Others argue that it is sometimes (11) (JUSTIFY), for example when someone feels unsafe or has been treated badly.

What most agree on is that a short, honest message is almost always (12) (PREFER) to silence. It does not need to be long or detailed. A simple "I don't think this is working, but I wish you well" can save the other person weeks of (13) (CERTAIN). As one psychologist puts it, "Closure is a form of (14) (KIND). It costs us a few seconds, and it shows that we respect the other person's (15) (FEEL)."

Interviewer: Tom, how long have you been a mountain rescue volunteer?

Tom: Eighteen years now. I joined when I was twenty-four, after I twisted my ankle on a mountain myself and had to be carried down. I was so grateful that I decided I wanted to give something back.

Interviewer: Are all the team members volunteers?

Tom: Every one of them. We have about forty members – teachers, farmers, a dentist, two nurses. Nobody is paid, and we even raise most of the money for our equipment ourselves. A new vehicle costs around sixty thousand pounds, so we spend a lot of weekends shaking collection boxes.

Interviewer: What happens when someone calls for help?

Tom: They ring 999 and ask for the police, who then contact us. Our phones beep, and whoever is free drops what they are doing. I've left a birthday party, a wedding and once even a dentist's chair with my mouth still numb. Usually we're on our way within fifteen minutes.

Interviewer: What kind of people do you rescue?

Tom: All kinds. Many are walkers who are lost or injured, often because they started too late in the day. In summer we see a lot of people in trainers who are not prepared for the weather, which can change very quickly up there. Mobile phones have changed things a lot. People use them to call us, but they also rely on them for maps, and then the battery dies.

Interviewer: What was your most difficult rescue?

Tom: A climber who fell at night in a snowstorm. It took us nine hours to reach him and bring him down. We couldn't use the helicopter because of the wind. He survived, and every Christmas he sends us a card. That makes it all worthwhile.

Interviewer: Any advice for our listeners?

Tom: Tell someone where you're going and when you expect to be back. And carry a paper map. It never runs out of battery.

You are going to listen to an interview with Dr Priya Shah, an ecologist who plants small forests in cities. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Dr Shah, what exactly is a tiny forest?

Dr Shah: It's a very dense forest about the size of a tennis court. The method comes from a Japanese botanist, Akira Miyawaki, who developed it in the 1970s. Instead of planting a few trees far apart, you plant around six hundred young trees very close together – three per square metre.

Interviewer: Why so close?

Dr Shah: Because the trees compete for light, so they grow upwards very fast – about ten times faster than in a normal plantation. After three years the forest needs no more care at all. We also use only native species, at least thirty different ones, so the forest is similar to the one that would have grown there naturally.

Interviewer: What are the benefits in a city?

Dr Shah: Many. A tiny forest can be several degrees cooler than the street next to it on a hot day. It absorbs rainwater, reduces noise and attracts wildlife. In our first forest in Leeds, volunteers counted over five hundred species of insects and animals within two years.

Interviewer: Who does the planting?

Dr Shah: Local people, especially schoolchildren. A planting day usually takes a single morning. We think it's important that people feel the forest belongs to them, so each forest has a group of "tree keepers" from the neighbourhood who collect data and organise events.

Interviewer: Are there any critics?

Dr Shah: Yes. Some foresters say the method is expensive, and that not all the trees will survive in such crowded conditions. That's true – some will die. But that is exactly what happens in a natural forest too.

Write a report of 150–180 words in which you:

  • describe your main tasks at the museum,
  • explain what you found most challenging and how you dealt with it,
  • recommend one change that would make the programme better for future volunteers.
To: Programme Organisers
From: Dominik(a) Novak
Subject: Volunteering at the City Museum
naloge.rezultat: Formalno poročilo z glavo, namenom, tremi odstavki s podnaslovi (naloge, izziv in rešitev, predlog izboljšave z utemeljitvijo) in sklepom; 150–180 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Zgradba poročila
To: Programme Organisers / From: Dominik(a) Novak / Subject: Volunteering at the City Museum
Glava in naslov.
Introduction: The aim of this report is to describe my four-week placement at the City Museum and to suggest an improvement.
Namen.
Main tasks
I guided groups of foreign tourists through the permanent exhibition and helped with children's workshops at weekends.
Konkretne naloge.
Challenges
The greatest challenge was answering detailed historical questions; I dealt with it by preparing notes with the curators and admitting politely when I did not know an answer.
Izziv + rešitev; višja raven: zapletenejše povedi.
Recommendation
I would recommend a short training course before the placement begins, as this would give new volunteers more confidence.
Predlog + utemeljitev.
Conclusion: Overall, the experience was extremely valuable, and I would encourage other students to take part.
Kratek sklep.

naloge.besedilo:
Discuss the role of Hailsham in Kazuo Ishiguro's Never Let Me Go.

Kazuo Ishiguro: Never Let Me Go

Write an essay of 250–300 words. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general.
naloge.rezultat: Esej o vlogi Hailshama: privilegirano otroštvo (umetnost, Galerija) in hkrati iluzija (»told and not told«), razkritje Miss Emily ter pomen Hailshama za Kathyjin spomin; 250–300 besed, brez obnove.
naloge.razlaga:
Načrt eseja
Uvod: teza – Hailsham is both a protective home and a carefully built illusion that prepares the students to accept their fate.
Teza na začetku; brez obnove.
Jedro 1 – a privileged childhood: art, Exchanges and the Gallery give the students a sense of being special; the guardians protect them from the outside world.
Konkretni prizori: Exchanges, Madame's Gallery.
Jedro 2 – 'told and not told': the students learn about donations gradually, so they never really question them; Miss Lucy is the only guardian who tells the truth.
Pokaži dvoumnost vzgoje.
Jedro 3 – Hailsham after Hailsham: Kathy keeps returning to it in memory; Miss Emily reveals it was an experiment to prove that clones have souls.
Razkritje na koncu spremeni pomen kraja.
Sklep: Hailsham gave its students a happy childhood but not freedom; it is the centre of Kathy's identity.
Vrnitev k tezi.
